extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, research-integrity professionals, sleuths/whistleblowers, and the scholarly publishing community
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and norms for drafting retraction notices and for whether/how publishers should acknowledge external 'sleuths' or whistleblowers whose investigations led to corrections or retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgment of external sleuths
rubrics_metrics.description: Should publishers acknowledge the work of sleuths when their work has led to retractions? (central question posed by the post)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece contrasts notices that omit sleuth-credit (Springer Nature example) with notices that explicitly cite and thank contributors (iJET citing Perron et al.). Best practice implied: when an external researcher or group provided evidence that led to an investigation/retraction, the retraction notice (or an associated public statement) should acknowledge that contribution so the record reflects who brought the issue to light.

rubrics_metrics.name: State specific reasons for retraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction notices should clearly state the factual grounds for retraction (e.g., 'evidence of peer review manipulation', 'authorship manipulation', 'acceptance based on illegitimate reviewer report').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in notices: Springer Nature's notice listing peer-review and authorship manipulation; Elsevier's notice explaining acceptance based on a fake reviewer account. Guidance: provide concrete, specific findings so readers understand why the record was corrected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of retraction actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Retract promptly when sufficient evidence is available; long delays signal problematic priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters observe that long delays 'given available evidence' harm credibility and signal publishers' priorities. Best practice: investigate and, if evidence warrants, update the publication record in a timely fashion rather than prolonged inaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain consent before publicly naming sleuths
rubrics_metrics.description: Before publishing any name (author or otherwise) the person should be contacted and asked if they want to be / should be named.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Debora Weber-Wulff's experience: being named without consent led to unwanted exposure and spam and even a PubMed listing. Best practice: contact the individual(s) to obtain informed consent before including names in notices or metadata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh safety/privacy risks of public attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicly naming sleuths can expose them to harassment or threats; publishers should consider these risks before attribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters point out incidents (e.g., harassment of Elisabeth Bik) and personal threats received after public identification. Guidance: balance credit with protection—if naming would create real danger or harassment, consider anonymized acknowledgement or private thanks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurately attribute the discovery of problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction notices and public statements should not misattribute the discovery of fraud to editors or institutional offices when external whistleblowers compiled the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: M. V. Dougherty notes whistleblower-compiled evidence is sometimes presented as the discovery of the RI office/editors. Best practice: clearly state who provided the original information and what role the publisher's investigation played in verifying it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat sleuthing as legitimate scholarly work deserving credit
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrating that a published article is fraudulent is itself a distinct form of scholarly research and merits recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters argue that sleuths' investigations are substantive scholarly contributions; policies could allow for citation, acknowledgement, or even formal publication of the investigative work so contributors receive appropriate credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishers should have robust internal fraud-detection processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers should not depend solely on volunteer sleuths; their peer-review and editorial processes must be able to detect paper-mill products and manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The omission of sleuth-credit 'means the journal ignores the fact that Springer Nature’s peer review process missed yet another paper mill paper.' Best practice: strengthen editorial controls, reviewer vetting, and detection tools so fewer problematic papers are published in the first place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep retraction notices focused on updating the publication record
rubrics_metrics.description: Publisher policy (per Springer Nature quoted) — 'In general we do not put thanks into retraction notes as the specific role of these notes is to update the publication record.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Springer Nature's stance: retraction notices should remain concise corrections of the literature; expressions of thanks are handled separately. The post presents this as a defensible policy but also shows counterexamples where notices included thanks; implementers must decide whether to keep notices strictly factual or also acknowledge contributors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide private or institutional thanks via Research Integrity teams
rubrics_metrics.description: When not including thanks in the public retraction note, publishers should contact and work directly with their Research Integrity teams to personally thank and coordinate with sleuths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Springer Nature suggests that when individuals 'contact and work directly with our Research Integrity team... they can personally thank the sleuths.' Best practice: ensure a mechanism for private acknowledgement, follow-up, and collaboration with contributors who assist investigations.
